strengths: Significance: Jointly improving deepfake detection and visually grounded explanations is a useful research objective. DF-R5's approximately 115,000 image–explanation pairs could provide a valuable resource for this specialized task.

Originality: Combining paragraph-level relative advantages with visual alignment and prediction-consistency rewards is a plausible extension of response-level RL. The label-free reward design is relevant to adaptation on unseen generators.

Empirical promise: The five leave-one-generator-out experiments report substantial improvements, including mean F1 increasing from 78.08 to 89.91 over DX-LLaVA. Reward-component ablations and comparisons with PPO and GRPO provide useful initial evidence.
Presentation: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies the 74-feature inventory, annotation and evaluation prompts, and PCR pseudocode.
weaknesses: Soundness—disconnected auxiliary supervision: Equation (1) and Figure 3 place the classifier directly on encoder features, before the projector. With the encoder frozen as specified in Section 4.1, the binary loss cannot update either the projector or Vicuna, contrary to the claimed mechanism behind Table 3. Equation (2) also omits the negative-class term of binary cross-entropy under its stated scalar binary formulation. The actual computation graph and loss require clarification.

Soundness—optimization objective: Equation (5) is explicitly maximized, while Equation (7) adds a positive KL penalty. Maximizing that sum encourages divergence; minimizing it reverses the policy-improvement objective. Paragraph probabilities also omit conditioning on preceding paragraphs, and their implementation as token products or normalized scores is unspecified. These ambiguities concern the central algorithm rather than peripheral notation.

Reproducibility and experimental validity: The test-time protocol does not specify whether adaptation is per image, per batch, or across an entire target domain; whether parameters reset; or when predictions are recorded. Rollout count, optimization steps, sampling settings, stopping criteria, and adaptation runtime are missing. Exact split sizes, identity/source overlap controls, and baseline training protocols are also unclear. Consequently, the fairness and practical cost of the reported generalization gains cannot be assessed. The promised code/data link is absent.

Quantitative reliability: Section 4.2 repeatedly describes 89.91 as accuracy, although Tables 4–5 identify it as F1 and report accuracy of 89.02. Table 10 contains more consequential inconsistencies: UnivCLIP on PixArt has precision 93.31 and recall 74.09 but F1 89.31, whereas their harmonic mean is approximately 82.60. The averaging conventions are not explained and appear inconsistent across methods. Tables 2 and 3 also give different precision values for the same baseline. Corrected metrics and uncertainty estimates are necessary to establish the claimed margins.

Explanation faithfulness is insufficiently validated: VCR measures global CLIP similarity to extracted keywords, which does not establish that a specific forensic artifact is present. PCR rewards lexical agreement rather than correctness. The sole quantitative explanation assessment uses GPT-4o, without reported evaluation sample size, uncertainty, human validation, or checks for judge/style bias. Moreover, annotation generation supplies ground-truth labels and re-prompts incorrect cases, potentially producing label-conditioned rationalizations. The reported 4.55 score therefore does not establish faithful visual reasoning.

Originality and causal attribution: Table 8 compares PRPO with PPO/GRPO using different reward designs, so it does not isolate the benefit of paragraph-level credit assignment. A GRPO baseline using the same VCR/PCR rewards and matched adaptation budget is needed. The RL comparison covers only DDIM and the reward ablation only SD, limiting evidence that the proposed mechanism explains the broader gains.

Limitations and research ethics: The evaluation is confined to five facial-image generation domains, without external-dataset or common image-degradation tests, yet the conclusions extend to reliable safety-critical use. The manuscript does not adequately discuss facial-data licensing/privacy, demographic performance, false accusations from incorrect detections, or the limitations of synthetic explanation supervision. These omissions reduce confidence in the dataset's responsible reuse and the claimed deployment relevance.

strengths: Significance: Explainable deepfake detection is a useful problem, and the paper addresses both classification and the reliability of accompanying explanations. DF-R5, with approximately 115,000 image–explanation pairs, could be a valuable resource if its annotation quality and release are established.

Originality: Assigning relative advantages to individual explanatory paragraphs is a plausible adaptation of GRPO to structured visual reasoning. Combining visual similarity with reasoning–prediction consistency provides a concrete, label-free reward design.

Empirical promise: The five held-out-generator experiments report improvements from DX-LLaVA to PRPO in every domain, increasing average F1 from 78.08 to 89.91 and accuracy from 84.64 to 89.02. The reward ablation on SD supports combining the two reward components.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies annotation prompts, the 74-feature vocabulary, the evaluation rubric, and PCR pseudocode. Backbone, learning rates, loss weights, and hardware are also specified.
weaknesses: Soundness—auxiliary supervision has an unresolved gradient-path problem. Equation (1) and Figure 3 attach the classifier directly to encoder features, before the projector; Section 4.1 freezes the encoder. Under this formulation, the binary loss updates only the classifier and cannot improve the projector or Vicuna as claimed in Section 3.2. The text instead describes a classifier on top of the projector. This discrepancy must be resolved to explain the gains in Table 3. Equation (2) also omits the negative-class term if its stated binary labels and scalar prediction are intended.

Soundness—the optimization objective is internally inconsistent. Equation (5) is a surrogate to maximize, while Equation (6) is a positive KL divergence intended to constrain policy drift; adding them in Equation (7) gives the wrong sign for one component under either minimization or maximization. Paragraph probabilities also omit conditioning on preceding paragraphs, and the implementation of paragraph likelihood ratios versus token-level clipping is unspecified. These ambiguities concern the central algorithm.

Reproducibility—the test-time protocol is insufficiently defined. The paper does not specify whether adaptation is per image, batch, or entire domain; whether weights reset between examples; the number of rollouts and updates; stopping/model-selection rules; or inference costs. Dataset split sizes, real-image provenance and overlap controls, and baseline training procedures are also unclear. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of whether comparisons use equivalent access to test data and compute. The promised code/dataset link is absent.

Evidence for explanation faithfulness is inadequate. Table 6 relies entirely on GPT-4o judging, without reporting the evaluation sample count, uncertainty, human validation, or judge agreement. Ground-truth labels are supplied during annotation refinement and reasoning generation, which can produce plausible post-hoc rationalizations without establishing that the cited artifacts exist. Keyword-level CLIP similarity and dictionary agreement likewise do not verify fine-grained forensic claims. Independent artifact-level validation is needed to support the central claims of reduced hallucination and faithful explanations.

The experiments do not isolate the paragraph-level contribution. PPO/GRPO comparisons appear only on DDIM, and Section 4.5 describes their sample-level majority-vote rewards rather than a clearly matched comparison using PRPO's reward signals and compute budget. Thus, reward design, optimization granularity, and adaptation effort are confounded. No repeated-run variability is reported. The ablations are useful preliminary evidence but do not establish general superiority over GRPO.

Presentation and numerical reliability: Section 4.2 repeatedly describes F1 values of 78.08 and 89.91 as accuracy, although Table 5 gives accuracies of 84.64 and 89.02. The claimed margin over Gemini is consequently overstated when interpreted as accuracy. Tables 2 and 3 give different precision values for the same baseline, and several Table 10 precision/recall/F1 combinations require explanation of their averaging conventions. These inconsistencies affect interpretation of the headline results.

Limitations and research ethics receive insufficient treatment. Evaluation covers five facial-image generation domains, with PRPO still reaching only 66.60% accuracy on SiT; this limits claims of robust generalization. The manuscript lacks substantive discussion of annotation bias, demographic error disparities, false accusations from confident explanations, and image licensing/privacy or redistribution conditions for DF-R5. These are relevant considerations for the proposed forensic use, although the manuscript provides no evidence of actual misconduct.

strengths: Significance: Improving both detection and explanations for synthetic facial images is a useful research goal. DF-R5's approximately 115k annotated images could provide a valuable resource for studying forensic reasoning.

Originality: Assigning paragraph-specific advantages using visual alignment and prediction consistency is a plausible, task-motivated extension of GRPO. The combination offers an interesting approach to adaptation without target labels.

Empirical merits: Table 4 reports substantial improvements across five held-out generator domains, increasing average F1 from 78.08 for DX-LLaVA to 89.91 with PRPO. The manuscript includes reward, backbone, and optimization ablations, alongside human evaluation and computational profiling.

Presentation and responsible framing: The pipeline is generally understandable, and the appendices provide annotation prompts, reward pseudocode, and architecture details. The limitations acknowledge face-centric coverage and dependence on Gemini, while the impact statement appropriately recommends decision support rather than autonomous decisions.
weaknesses: Soundness—auxiliary-loss mechanism: Equation (1) and Figure 3 attach the classifier directly to pooled encoder features, while the encoder is frozen. Consequently, the binary loss has no gradient path to the projector or Vicuna and cannot improve their discrimination as claimed in Section 3.2. The prose instead describes a classifier above the projector. This discrepancy must be resolved to explain the substantial auxiliary-loss gains. Equation (3) also omits the negative-class term of binary cross-entropy unless an unstated vector-label convention is intended.

Soundness—reported metrics: Table 17 contains material inconsistencies. For UnivCLIP on SiT, precision 71.53 and recall 83.03 imply binary F1 approximately 76.85, whereas the reported F1 is 40.01; on PixArt, the corresponding implied F1 is 82.60 rather than 89.31. Alternative averaging conventions are not specified and would need to be consistent across methods. SIDA's five listed F1 scores average to 75.56, not the 75.26 used for the headline 14.65-point improvement. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the comparative results.

Reproducibility—test-time optimization: The manuscript does not adequately specify adaptation steps, rollout count for the main experiments, sampling settings, checkpoint selection, whether weights reset per image or persist across a domain, or when predictions are measured relative to adaptation. Equations (9)–(11) also leave paragraph probabilities and conditioning on preceding paragraphs unclear. Epoch counts, complete reward dictionaries, and identity/source-disjoint splitting details are missing. The sentence announcing code and dataset availability provides no actual location.

Originality and causal attribution: Table 8 compares PRPO's new rewards and paragraph-level optimization against PPO/GRPO using final-answer majority-vote rewards. This does not isolate the contribution of paragraph-level optimization. A matched-reward, matched-compute GRPO comparison is needed, together with a sampling-only baseline. The supervised-versus-unsupervised comparison likewise does not clearly establish that both methods adapt on the same data under the same protocol.

Soundness—visual faithfulness: CLIP similarity to YAKE keywords measures semantic compatibility, which need not distinguish an observed forensic artifact from a plausible but false description. Appendix B.1 measures prediction degradation under image corruptions, rather than whether VCR distinguishes correct and incorrect artifact descriptions; those results therefore do not establish the claimed fine-grained grounding. Controlled contradictory descriptions, artifact localization, or targeted counterfactual tests would directly test this central claim.

Evidence quality—reasoning annotations and evaluation: Annotation generation supplies ground-truth labels and retains supporting features, creating a risk of label-conditioned rationalization that is not independently audited at scale. GPT-4o judging and eight participants rating only five images each provide limited evidence for general explanation faithfulness. No inter-rater agreement or uncertainty is reported, and this small study cannot establish the claimed reliability and lack of bias of the automated judge. Detection results also lack repeated-run uncertainty.

Significance and practical limits: Evaluation is confined to five facial-generation domains within the constructed benchmark. This specialization is reasonable, but broad robustness and state-of-the-art claims require stronger external validation. The reported approximately 30.72-point accuracy drop under JPEG compression is practically consequential. Profiling on eight H200 GPUs is useful, but without total adaptation cost and matched baseline costs it does not establish practical test-time efficiency. Dataset licensing, facial-data privacy, and demographic performance also receive insufficient discussion.

strengths: Significance: Explainable deepfake detection is a useful problem. DF-R5’s approximately 115,000 image–explanation pairs and structured annotation pipeline could provide a valuable resource for face-focused forensic reasoning.

Originality: Combining paragraph-level policy advantages with visual alignment and prediction-consistency rewards is a plausible, task-specific extension of GRPO that does not require test-time labels.

Empirical promise: Table 4 reports an average F1 improvement from 78.08 for DX-LLaVA to 89.91 with PRPO across five held-out generators. The manuscript includes reward, architecture, and RL-baseline ablations, alongside computational profiling.

Presentation and limitations: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix provides annotation prompts, feature lists, reward pseudocode, and architecture details. The authors appropriately acknowledge the face-centric scope, dependence on Gemini annotations, and difficulties with sparse artifacts.
weaknesses: Soundness—disconnected auxiliary objective: Equation (1) and Figure 3 attach the classifier directly to pooled encoder features, while the encoder is frozen. Under this formulation, the binary loss cannot update either the projector or Vicuna, contradicting the claimed mechanism and improvements in Table 3. The text instead says the classifier is placed after the projector. These are materially different architectures, and the manuscript must establish which was implemented. Equation (3) also omits the negative-class term of binary cross-entropy unless an unstated vector-label convention is intended.

Reproducibility—test-time adaptation is underspecified: The paper does not clearly establish whether updates occur separately per image, cumulatively across batches, or through repeated passes over the held-out domain; when weights reset; or how many updates precede evaluation. Essential rollout and optimization settings are missing. Section 4.9 further describes supervised versus unsupervised PRPO as training on four domains, leaving their relationship to the test-time protocol unclear. These details determine both the meaning and reproducibility of the central generalization results. The stated code/data availability sentence also lacks a usable link.

Soundness—visual faithfulness remains insufficiently established: VCR measures global CLIP similarity to YAKE keywords, which need not distinguish a correctly observed artifact from a plausible but absent one, especially after qualifiers or negations are removed. Appendix B.1 measures prediction degradation under image corruptions; this does not isolate whether VCR recognizes correct forensic descriptions. Controlled comparisons against mismatched, negated, and hallucinated explanations, validated by independent annotations, are needed to support the claimed grounding mechanism.

Evaluation—explanation validation is too limited for the claims: The main evidence is GPT-4o scoring. Human validation comprises eight participants rating only five images each, with no uncertainty estimates or inter-rater agreement. This cannot establish the assertion in Appendix D.1 that the judge is reliable and unbiased. Ground-truth-conditioned annotation generation also risks producing post-hoc rationalizations; classification correctness and low n-gram overlap do not validate the truth of individual visual claims.

Attribution and originality: Table 8 compares PRPO with TTRL-style PPO/GRPO using different reward constructions, so it does not isolate the benefit of paragraph-level optimization. A matched GRPO baseline using the same VCR/PCR information, rollout budget, and adaptation schedule is necessary. A simple paragraph-vote correction baseline would also help distinguish learned improvements from enforcing answer consistency.

Quantitative reliability and presentation: Table 17 contains unexplained metric inconsistencies. For example, UnivCLIP on SiT has precision 71.53 and recall 83.03 but F1 40.01; their standard binary harmonic mean is approximately 76.85. Other baseline rows also require clarification of averaging conventions. The DDIM LLaVA F1 differs between Tables 4 and 9 without a clear explanation, and Table 19’s default beta result differs from the main PRPO result. No repeated-run uncertainty is provided. These issues weaken confidence in the reported comparative margins.

Practical significance and ethics: Profiling reports approximately 7.4 seconds per sample per adaptation iteration even at batch size 32 on eight H200 GPUs, but total adaptation cost and a matched inference-cost comparison are absent. Dataset documentation also does not adequately specify identity/source overlap controls, redistribution permissions, or demographic performance. These omissions matter for reproducibility and the proposed forensic use, although the manuscript does not itself establish an ethical violation.

strengths: Significance: Explainable deepfake detection is a useful problem, and DF-R5’s approximately 115,000 image–explanation pairs could provide a valuable resource for studying structured forensic explanations.

Originality: Assigning relative advantages to individual reasoning paragraphs, using visual alignment and prediction consistency without test labels, is a meaningful adaptation of group-relative policy optimization to this application.

Empirical promise: Table 4 reports an average F1 increase from 78.08 for DX-LLaVA to 89.91 with PRPO across five held-out generators. Backbone, reward-component, and architecture-transfer ablations provide useful initial evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies annotation prompts, reward pseudocode, architecture details, and computational profiling. The paper appropriately acknowledges its face-centric scope, dependence on Gemini annotations, and risks of treating generated explanations as authoritative.
weaknesses: Soundness—an unresolved gradient-flow problem affects the architectural contribution. Equation (1) applies the auxiliary classifier directly to pooled encoder features, and Figure 3 likewise branches the classifier before the projector. Because the encoder is frozen, the binary loss cannot update either the projector or Vicuna under this formulation. This contradicts the claimed mechanism behind Tables 3 and 10. Equation (3) also omits the negative-class term of binary cross-entropy unless an unstated vector-label convention is intended. The implemented computation graph and loss need clarification.

Soundness—the central grounding claim is insufficiently validated. VCR measures global CLIP similarity to YAKE keywords, which need not preserve negation or distinguish an observed artifact from a plausible description. PCR rewards agreement rather than correctness. Appendix B.1 measures detection degradation under image perturbations, not whether VCR ranks accurate explanations above matched hallucinations. These results do not establish fine-grained forensic grounding; controlled counterfactual descriptions and independently annotated artifact judgments are needed.

Evaluation—the explanation study is too limited to establish faithfulness. GPT-4o supplies the principal scores, while the human study has eight participants rating only five images each, without uncertainty estimates or inter-rater agreement. This cannot substantiate Appendix D.1’s claim that the automated evaluator is reliable and unbiased. Ground-truth-conditioned annotation generation also risks producing label-consistent rationalizations. Linguistic diversity and high rubric scores do not resolve whether individual claims are visually correct.

Reproducibility—the test-time adaptation protocol is materially underspecified. The manuscript does not clearly establish the number of optimization steps, rollout count for the main experiments, reset versus continual adaptation behavior, checkpoint selection, or whether an image is evaluated before or after updates using that image. Paragraph probabilities in Equations (9)–(11) omit preceding-paragraph conditioning and do not explain token aggregation or length normalization. Section 4.9 also leaves unclear whether supervised and unsupervised PRPO receive comparable adaptation data. These details determine both validity and deployment cost.

Attribution and comparison—the PPO/GRPO comparison in Table 8 changes reward construction as well as credit assignment, so it does not isolate the benefit of paragraph-level optimization. A GRPO baseline with the same VCR/PCR rewards and matched sampling and update budgets is needed, together with a sampling-only baseline. The largest improvement occurs on SiT, but the RL-method comparison is restricted to DDIM. No repeated-run variability is reported.

Reporting and reproducibility—several numerical inconsistencies require resolution. Table 17 gives UnivCLIP precision 93.31, recall 74.09, and F1 89.31 on PixArt; these cannot arise from conventional binary F1, and consistent averaging conventions are not specified. Table 19 reports 93.60 F1 at the stated default beta of 0.01, versus 95.88 in the main DDIM result. Tables 4 and 17 also disagree on SIDA’s average F1. Dataset split counts, identity/source separation, and filtering outcomes need fuller documentation, and the promised code/data link is absent. These issues, together with the unresolved methodological concerns, prevent the otherwise promising reported gains from supporting acceptance.
